newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's market watchdog investigation nearly complete.
newsitem.headline: HK's market watchdog investigation nearly complete.

text.p: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) has almost completed its investigation into unusual trading activity in the Hong Kong market on November 28 last year, a legislative council panel was told on Monday.

"The SFC said today that they have almost completed the investigation into the November incident where there were wild swings of the market," said Huang Chen Ya, chairman of the Financial Affairs Panel of the Legislative Council (Legco).
"They (the SFC) are going to talk to the exchange about it and hope to come out with a public statement in about one or two months' time, " Huang added.
The Hang Seng Index surged 213 points to a then all time high of 13,744.30 in the first 15 minutes of trade on November 28.
Brokers said at the time there appeared to be massive programme trading at the open, possibly related to the expiry of the November Hang Seng index futures contract later that day.
The exchange examined the opening transactions of a number of stocks and questioned brokers involved in those transactions, stock exchange officials said in November.
The SFC later took up its own investigation.
Acting commission chief executive Michael Wu told the Legco panel meeting the SFC was looking into quite a few suspected cases of market manipulation.
"They said they have looked at about 100 cases of market manipulation in the past, and of those about 50 cases have to be investigated further," said Huang.
They were still in the process of looking at some of these cases and could not provide any additional information, Huang said councillors were told.
The panel asked the commission about speculation in red chips, Huang said.

They also asked whether there was market manipulation of these China plays and whether the SFC had failed to look into this market because it was afraid to tackle this politically sensitive sector of the market, Huang said.

"They said because the whole market for red chips was going up at that time, therefore even though some red chips seemed to have risen inordinately (high), it probably could only be interpreted as part of the rising tide," said Huang
The SFC also said they had found no strong evidence that brokers were involved but that certain brokerages seemed to have a lot of participation in the rapid ascent of some stocks, Huang said.

Huang said that it was much more difficult to prove cases of market manipulation by brokers and that the brokers should be encouraged to warn clients of the risks of investing in stocks that had already risen well above their underlying asset value.
There should be guidelines for brokers and those that were found to be misleading their clients should be penalised, Huang said.
